segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Owen Vane parted with his dispensing book as a man parts with a finger. He wrapped it in oilcloth himself, and tied the string himself, and told his sister twice that there were four years of accounts in it besides the entry she wanted, and that if it went into a ditch he might as well shut the shop.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith carried it across the green to the Bell on Monday evening and laid it on the table in the parlour, and beside it she set down, in as few words as she could manage, everything Mrs Whitlow had said in the kitchen at Oakmere. Farr heard her out without moving.

segments.speaker: Captain Farr
segments.text: April. She wrote in April, and I was in Portsmouth by August with nothing to do but sit.

segments.speaker: Miss Vane
segments.text: She cannot swear it was sent.

segments.speaker: Captain Farr
segments.text: No. But my great-uncle's papers are lodged with an attorney in Winchester, Mr Tredgold, in Jewry Street. He drew the old will, the one that named me, and he must have the newer one now, and he has never once written to me either. I shall go to him Wednesday and put the whole of it in his hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mr Rowe had come in for the sake of the fire, having no fire of his own worth the name, and had been quiet for a full quarter of an hour, which for him was a considerable achievement. He now made a noise like a man about to apologize.

segments.speaker: Mr Rowe
segments.text: You will forgive me. Only I have been turning it about, and if you go alone, sir, what does the gentleman see? He sees a half-pay officer with a limp and a thin coat, come back from the dead a fortnight after a farm worth three hundred a year has gone elsewhere, telling a very convenient story about a book he has not got and a letter nobody can produce. He will be perfectly civil. He will do nothing whatever.

segments.speaker: Captain Farr
segments.text: That is a hard way of putting it.

segments.speaker: Mr Rowe
segments.text: It is his way of putting it. I only say it first, so that it does you less damage. But if Miss Vane goes, and the book is in her keeping and not in yours, and she is the apothecary's own sister and has no claim on the farm and never can have one—then it is not a story. It is testimony, and it comes from somebody with nothing to gain by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith looked at the oilcloth parcel for some time.

segments.speaker: Miss Vane
segments.text: Wednesday, then. There is a chaise to be had at the Bell for eighteen shillings and we may be back before dark.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike had the whole of it before breakfast on Tuesday, and gave her opinion in the library, on the green, and at the draper's counter, where it was best attended.

segments.speaker: Mrs Pike
segments.text: Eleven miles in a closed carriage with a man nobody here has laid eyes on these thirteen years. I do not say he is not everything he ought to be. I say she has no mother living and her brother has no more sense than a pestle, and there is not a soul in this parish who will remember the book and every soul who will remember the carriage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith heard it from four separate people and made no answer to any of them, which Mrs Pike afterwards described as sullenness and Mr Rowe as courage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They left at eight on Wednesday. The road runs west out of Amberlight and is tolerable as far as the turning, and past the turning it is ruts baked hard in September and never mended since. Farr sat with his hands on his knees and named the farms as they went by, and Judith kept the parcel on her lap and did not put it down once.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three miles short of Winchester there was a crack like a musket, and the chaise went over to the near side and stopped with the shafts pointing at the hedge. Nobody was hurt. The wheel lay in the road eight feet behind them with two spokes out of it and the felloe split from rim to nave.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The driver walked back, picked the wheel up, looked at it, and put it down again.

segments.speaker: Miss Vane
segments.text: How long?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man took his hat off and scratched his head and looked up the empty road toward Winchester and down the empty road toward Alresford.

segments.speaker: Captain Farr
segments.text: There is the carrier. He goes through of an evening.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The driver shook his head.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The carrier had gone through on Monday, said the man, and would not go again until Friday, and the Winchester coach did not come this way at all. There was a wheelwright at Itchen Abbas who might be fetched, and might be found sober, and might come out tonight, though he would not swear to any of the three. Nothing else would pass before morning.
